name: Docker Basics
author: Recurse
subject: tools
description: Build images, run containers, publish ports, keep data in volumes, and connect services with Compose.

lesson.intro: Docker packages an application with everything it needs to run, so it behaves the same on a laptop, a CI server and production. This lesson covers images and containers, Dockerfiles that build fast, ports, volumes and configuration, networking with Docker Compose, and keeping images small.

sections.title: Images, containers and everyday commands
sections.body:
An image is a read-only template: a filesystem built from layers, plus settings such as the default command. A container is a running instance of an image. Docker gives each container its own thin writable layer on top of the image, so many containers can share one image without affecting each other.

Anything a container writes goes into its writable layer. Stopping and starting the container keeps that data, but `docker rm` deletes it. The image itself never changes.

Images are named `name:tag`, such as `nginx:1.27`. If you leave the tag off, Docker uses `latest`, which is only a label, not a promise of the newest version. Pin versions for repeatable setups.

- `docker run` creates and starts a container. `-d` runs it in the background, `--name` names it, `--rm` deletes it when it exits, and `-it` gives you an interactive terminal.
- `docker ps` lists running containers; `docker ps -a` includes stopped ones.
- `docker logs name` shows what the main process printed; `-f` follows it live.
- `docker exec -it name sh` runs a command, here a shell, inside a running container.
- `docker stop`, `docker start` and `docker rm` stop, restart and delete a container.

A container runs only as long as its main process. When that process exits, because the job finished or the app crashed, the container stops.
sections.code:
docker pull nginx:1.27             # download an image
docker images                      # list local images
docker run -d --name web nginx:1.27
docker ps                          # running containers
docker logs web                    # output of the main process
docker exec -it web sh             # shell inside the running container
docker stop web                    # stopped, but it still exists
docker ps -a                       # also lists stopped containers
docker rm web                      # deletes the container, not the image
sections.tip: Use `docker run --rm` for one-off commands so stopped containers do not pile up.

check.question: Starting with no nginx image on the machine, you run `docker run -d nginx` three times. What do you have now?
choices: Three images and three containers
One image and one container
Three images and one container
One image and three containers
check.explanation: The image is downloaded once and reused. Each docker run creates a new container from it, each with its own writable layer.

sections.title: Dockerfiles and layer caching
sections.body:
A Dockerfile is the recipe for an image. The most common instructions:

- `FROM` picks the base image to start from.
- `WORKDIR` sets the directory that later instructions, and the container, work in. It is created if needed.
- `COPY src dest` copies files from the build context into the image.
- `RUN` executes a command while the image is being built, such as installing packages.
- `ENV` sets an environment variable for later steps and for the running container.
- `EXPOSE` documents which port the app listens on. It does not publish the port.
- `CMD` sets the default command a container runs when it starts.

Build with `docker build -t myapp:1.0 .`. The final `.` is the build context: the directory whose files `COPY` can see.

Each instruction produces a layer, and Docker caches layers. On a rebuild it reuses a layer when the instruction and the files it uses have not changed. As soon as one step changes, every step after it runs again. So put slow steps that rarely change, like installing dependencies, before steps that change often, like copying your source code.
sections.code:
FROM node:20-slim
WORKDIR /app
# Dependencies change rarely, so install them first
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
# Source code changes often, so copy it last
COPY . .
ENV NODE_ENV=production
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
sections.tip: Dockerfile comments must be on their own line. Text after an instruction, even after a #, is passed to that instruction.

check.question: With the Dockerfile above, you edit only server.js and rebuild. Which steps run again instead of coming from the cache?
choices: COPY . . and every step after it
Every step, starting from FROM
Only RUN npm ci
None, because Docker cannot see source changes
check.explanation: The package files did not change, so their COPY and RUN npm ci are reused. COPY . . sees a changed file, so it and all later steps rebuild.

sections.title: Ports, volumes and configuration
sections.body:
Each container has its own network interface, so a server on port 80 inside it cannot be reached from your machine until you publish the port. `-p 8080:80` maps port 8080 on the host to port 80 in the container: host first, container second.

The app inside must listen on `0.0.0.0` (all interfaces). If it listens on `127.0.0.1`, it accepts connections only from inside its own container, and the published port leads nowhere.

Data written inside a container disappears when the container is removed. To keep it, mount storage:

- A named volume, `-v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data`, is storage managed by Docker. It survives `docker rm` and can be attached to a new container.
- A bind mount, `-v "$PWD":/app`, maps a folder on your machine into the container. Edits on either side appear on the other, which is handy during development.

Pass configuration such as database URLs and passwords at run time with `-e NAME=value` or `--env-file .env`. Values set with `ENV` in a Dockerfile are stored in the image, and anyone who has the image can read them with `docker inspect`.
sections.code:
docker run -d --name db \
  -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=devpass \
  -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data \
  -p 5432:5432 \
  postgres:16
docker rm -f db         # the container is gone...
docker volume ls        # ...but the pgdata volume and its data remain
sections.tip: Remember the order in -p as "outside:inside": the host port comes first.

check.question: Why pass a database password with `-e` when running the container instead of `ENV` in the Dockerfile?
choices: ENV cannot hold values longer than eight characters
-e encrypts the value so other processes cannot read it
ENV values are saved in the image, readable by anyone who has it
Apps inside the container cannot read variables set with ENV
check.explanation: ENV becomes part of the image config, visible through docker inspect and to anyone you share the image with. -e supplies the value only to that one container at run time.

sections.title: Networking and Docker Compose
sections.body:
Containers on the same user-defined network can reach each other by name, because Docker runs a small DNS service for that network. Inside a container, `localhost` means that container itself, not your machine and not the other containers. Published ports are for reaching a container from the host; containers talking to each other on a shared network do not need them.

Docker Compose describes a multi-container app in one `compose.yaml` file. Each service becomes a container, and Compose puts all of them on one network where the service name works as a hostname.

- `docker compose up -d` builds or pulls the images, creates the network and volumes, and starts everything in the background.
- `docker compose logs -f web` follows one service's output.
- `docker compose down` stops and removes the containers and the network. Named volumes are kept unless you add `-v`.
sections.code:
services:
  web:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "8080:3000"
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://app:secret@db:5432/app
    depends_on:
      - db
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: app
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
      POSTGRES_DB: app
    volumes:
      - dbdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
volumes:
  dbdata:
sections.tip: `depends_on` only controls start order. It does not wait until the database is ready to accept connections.

check.question: Which command stops and removes the containers and network of this app but keeps the data in the dbdata volume?
choices: docker compose down -v
docker compose down
docker compose stop
docker volume rm dbdata
check.explanation: down removes containers and the network but leaves named volumes alone. Adding -v also deletes the volumes. stop only stops the containers without removing them.

sections.title: Small images and .dockerignore
sections.body:
Smaller images download faster, start faster, and contain fewer packages that could have security holes.

- Start from a slim base, such as `python:3.12-slim` or an `alpine` variant, instead of the full image.
- Clean up in the same `RUN` step that made the mess. Every layer is stored in the image; deleting files in a later layer only hides them.
- Use a multi-stage build: compile in a large build stage, then copy only the result into a small final stage.

A `.dockerignore` file lists paths to leave out of the build context, using patterns like `.gitignore`. For a Node project it might list `node_modules`, `.git`, `*.log` and `.env`. This keeps the context small so builds start quickly, keeps secrets out of images, and stops `COPY . .` from busting the cache when an unrelated file changes.
sections.code:
# Build stage: full Node toolchain and dev dependencies
FROM node:20 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

# Final stage: just a web server and the built files
FROM nginx:1.27-alpine
COPY --from=build /app/dist /usr/share/nginx/html
sections.tip: Run `docker images` before and after a change to see what it did to the image size.

check.question: A Dockerfile has `RUN apt-get install -y build-essential` and, in a later step, `RUN apt-get purge -y build-essential`. Why is the image still large?
choices: The earlier layer keeps the files; the later one only hides them
apt-get purge removes packages but never deletes their files
Docker only compresses the final layer, so earlier ones stay big
The image must be rebuilt with --no-cache to apply the purge
check.explanation: Layers are stacked, never edited. The install layer keeps its files forever, and the purge layer just marks them deleted. Installing, using and removing in one RUN avoids that.

keyTerms.definition: A read-only, layered template containing a filesystem and settings such as the default command.
A running (or stopped) instance of an image with its own writable layer.
The filesystem change made by one Dockerfile instruction; layers are cached and reused between builds.
The files sent to Docker for a build, usually the directory given as the last argument of docker build.
Docker-managed storage mounted into a container that survives the container being removed.
A host port mapped to a container port with -p HOST:CONTAINER.
One container definition in compose.yaml; its name doubles as a hostname on the app network.
A Dockerfile with several FROM stages, where the final image copies only what it needs from earlier ones.

summary: An image is a read-only, layered template; a container is a running instance with its own writable layer.
Order Dockerfile steps from least to most often changed so the layer cache can skip slow steps like dependency installs.
`-p HOST:CONTAINER` publishes a port, named volumes keep data after `docker rm`, and `-e` passes configuration at run time.
Containers on a shared network, such as Compose services, reach each other by name; `localhost` inside a container is that container.
Slim bases, multi-stage builds and a `.dockerignore` keep images small, fast to build, and free of secrets.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only run apps directly on their laptop the difference between an image and a container, and why the order of lines in a Dockerfile changes how fast it rebuilds.

questions.question: You start a container from `ubuntu`, install curl inside it, then `docker rm` it and start a new container from `ubuntu`. Is curl installed in the new one?
choices: Yes; installing a package inside a container updates the image
No; the install lived in the removed container's writable layer
Yes, but only if the new container gets the same name
No, because package managers do not work inside containers
questions.explanation: Images never change when containers run. The install went into the first container's writable layer, which docker rm deleted. To keep it, add a RUN step to a Dockerfile and build a new image.

questions.question: Type the command that lists all containers, including stopped ones.
questions.explanation: docker ps shows only running containers. -a adds stopped ones along with their exit status.

questions.question: The container seems to vanish right after starting. What should you check first?
questions.code:
docker run -d --name worker myworker:1.0
docker ps
CONTAINER ID   IMAGE   COMMAND   CREATED   STATUS   PORTS   NAMES
choices: docker exec -it worker sh, to look around inside the container
docker pull myworker:1.0, since the image must be missing
docker logs worker, since the main process likely exited
Run it again with -p, since detached containers need a port
questions.explanation: A container stops when its main process exits, and docker ps hides stopped containers. docker logs still works on a stopped container and usually shows the error. docker exec only works on running containers.

questions.question: Type the command that shows the output of a container named `api` and keeps following new lines as they arrive.
questions.explanation: docker logs prints what the container's main process wrote to stdout and stderr. -f (follow) keeps the stream open, like tail -f.

questions.question: What is the difference between RUN and CMD in a Dockerfile?
choices: RUN runs at build time; CMD runs when a container starts
RUN starts the app; CMD runs shell commands during the build
RUN runs as root; CMD always runs as a normal user
They do the same thing, but CMD is the newer syntax
questions.explanation: RUN steps happen once, at build time, and their results are saved in layers. CMD is stored as metadata and runs each time a container starts, unless you pass a different command to docker run.

questions.question: Every code change makes this build reinstall all dependencies, which takes minutes. What is the fix?
questions.code:
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
CMD ["python", "app.py"]
choices: Replace COPY with ADD so the files are cached
Move CMD above RUN so the app starts before the install
Add EXPOSE so Docker can cache the install layer
Copy requirements.txt and run pip install before COPY . .
questions.explanation: COPY . . changes whenever any file changes, and everything after it rebuilds, including pip install. Copying only requirements.txt first lets the install layer stay cached until the requirements change.

questions.question: Complete the instruction so the later COPY, RUN and CMD steps all work inside /app.
questions.code:
FROM node:20-slim
_____ /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
choices: CD
WORKDIR
RUN cd
ENV
questions.explanation: WORKDIR sets the working directory for every following instruction and for the container. RUN cd /app would only last for that single RUN step, and CD is not an instruction.

questions.question: What does `EXPOSE 3000` in a Dockerfile do?
choices: Publishes port 3000 on the host automatically
Blocks every port in the container except 3000
Documents the app's port; it does not publish it
Starts the app and tells it to listen on 3000
questions.explanation: EXPOSE is documentation stored in the image. Nothing is reachable from the host until you publish a port with -p (or -P, which publishes exposed ports to random host ports).

questions.question: You ran `docker run -d -p 8080:80 nginx`. Which address on your machine reaches nginx?
choices: http://localhost:8080
http://localhost:80
http://nginx:8080
http://localhost:8080:80
questions.explanation: In -p 8080:80 the host port comes first and the container port second, so the host listens on 8080 and forwards to nginx on port 80 inside the container.

questions.question: The container runs with `-p 3000:3000`, but requests from the host to localhost:3000 fail. What is the bug in the app?
choices: Port 3000 is reserved by Docker, so the app must use another one
createServer needs the host port 3000 passed as a second argument
res.end must be res.send, or Docker will not forward the response
It binds to 127.0.0.1, reachable only from inside the container
questions.explanation: Docker forwards published traffic to the container's network interface, not to its loopback. A server bound to 127.0.0.1 never sees it. Binding to 0.0.0.0 accepts connections on every interface.

questions.question: Complete the command so the database files survive deleting and recreating the container.
choices: -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
--restart always
-e PGDATA=/var/lib/postgresql/data
questions.explanation: A named volume mounted at Postgres's data directory stores the files outside the container's writable layer, so a new container can mount the same data. --restart always restarts the same container but does nothing once it is deleted, and PGDATA only changes where Postgres writes inside the container.

questions.question: In a Compose app, the web service connects to `localhost:5432` and gets "connection refused". The database is the service named db. Why?
choices: Compose services can only reach each other through published ports
Port 5432 must also be listed under the web service's ports
Inside the web container, localhost is web itself; connect to db:5432
The database refuses connections until depends_on is added
questions.explanation: Every container has its own localhost. Compose puts services on a shared network where each service name resolves to that container, so the database is at db:5432. Published ports are only for the host.

questions.question: Type the command that starts every service in compose.yaml in the background.
questions.explanation: up creates the network, volumes and containers (building or pulling images if needed) and starts them; -d detaches so you get your terminal back.

questions.question: The web service has `depends_on: [db]`, yet it sometimes crashes at startup because it cannot reach Postgres. Why?
choices: depends_on is ignored unless the db service publishes its port
Compose puts each service on its own separate network by default
depends_on starts db after web, the reverse of what is needed
depends_on orders startup but does not wait for Postgres to be ready
questions.explanation: Compose starts the db container first, but Postgres needs a few seconds before it accepts connections. Handle it with retries in the app, or a healthcheck plus depends_on with condition: service_healthy.

questions.question: Complete the final stage so it copies only the compiled binary out of the build stage.
questions.code:
FROM golang:1.23 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /out/server .

FROM alpine:3.20
_____ /out/server /usr/local/bin/server
CMD ["server"]
choices: COPY --from=build
COPY build:
FROM build COPY
ADD --stage=build
questions.explanation: COPY --from=<stage> copies files from an earlier stage instead of the build context. The Go toolchain and source stay behind in the build stage, so the final image is a small Alpine base plus one binary.

questions.question: The build crawls while Docker sends almost 1 GB of context, and the image ends up containing the developer's .env file. What is missing?
questions.code:
ls -a
.  ..  .env  .git  Dockerfile  node_modules  package.json  src
docker build -t app .
 => => transferring context: 912.40MB
choices: A smaller, slim base image in the FROM line
The --no-cache flag added to docker build
A .dockerignore for node_modules, .git and .env
A WORKDIR instruction before the COPY step
questions.explanation: Without a .dockerignore, everything in the directory is sent as build context and COPY . . puts it all in the image. Ignoring node_modules, .git and .env makes the context small and keeps secrets out.

questions.question: Why does a multi-stage build usually produce a much smaller image?
questions.answer: The final stage starts from a fresh, small base and copies in only the build output. Compilers, dev dependencies and source files stay in the earlier stage, which is not part of the final image.
questions.explanation: Only the last stage becomes the image you ship. Earlier stages are used during the build and then left behind.
